title: How to pitch a reported essay to an editor
description: Write a pitch that shows the scene, the question and how you’ll report it. Includes a sample email and a checklist for choosing an editor.
intro: A reported essay starts with something you’ve noticed and follows it beyond your own experience. To pitch one, give an editor a scene they can picture, a question worth answering and a credible way to answer it. Here’s how that works with an ordinary subject: the last bus home.

sections.heading: Find the question inside the scene
paragraphs: “I’d like to write about public transport” gives an editor a subject. Try narrowing it to one stop and one decision. Imagine a kitchen porter hanging up their apron at eleven. The last bus left at ten fifty. Who gets to work a closing shift when getting home costs more than the last hour’s pay? Now there’s a question a reader can carry through the piece.

Make two notes before you draft. In the first, write what you could describe from your own experience. In the second, put the claim that still needs checking. You may remember the silence at a bus stop. To say a route misses the end of a shift, you need the timetable for the right day, a shift time and someone who actually makes that journey.

sections.heading: Choose the section before you write the email
paragraphs: Read two recent pieces in the section you have in mind. Does the writer appear in the story? How far does each piece travel beyond its opening scene? A transport desk might want the timetable decision investigated. An essays editor might want to know what the walk home taught you about who can afford to stay in a job.

Check the publication’s current instructions. Some editors invite ideas, while others want the finished essay. Follow their requested format, destination and length. If you already have a draft, say so. If you’re proposing interviews, say which conversations you’ve had and which you still hope to arrange.

sections.heading: A sample pitch email
paragraphs: This fictional example shows how a writer could describe their access without promising an interview on someone else’s behalf.
Subject: Essay pitch — The shift that ends ten minutes after the last bus

Hi Jo, I used to keep a pair of trainers under the sink at the restaurant where I washed dishes. On Sundays I could change shoes and walk home or spend my last hour’s wages on a taxi. I’d like to write a reported essay for your Working Life section about the quiet calculation behind taking a closing shift.

I still have my old rotas. I’d compare them with the bus timetable from that period, then travel the route on a Sunday night to see what has changed. One former colleague has agreed to talk. I’d also ask a manager how closing shifts are allocated and invite the bus operator to explain its timetable. If our experiences differ, that difference belongs in the piece.
I’m proposing 1,200 words, opening with the shoes and ending at the stop as the next shift clocks off. I could file three weeks after commissioning. Would that work for your section? Best, Alex.

sections.heading: Give the pitch one last edit
paragraphs: Read the email aloud. If the opening could describe any town or any writer, restore one detail only you would know. If a sentence predicts what a source will say, replace it with the question you’ll ask. Link a relevant writing sample if the editor requests one. Check that it opens without a login.

An editor should be able to tell what readers will discover, why you can tell the story and what remains uncertain. Save a copy with the outlet’s response window. If the outlet publishes a follow-up policy, use it to decide when to check back.
